pr_title: [7.0] Disable body streams for H2 CONNECT requests
pr_body:
Disallow reading the request body or writing to the response body for H2 CONNECT requests.

## Description

HTTP/2 CONNECT requests use a new protocol implemented in 7.0 to enable WebSockets over HTTP/2. When the request is presented to the application the normal request and response body streams and pipe reader/writers let you interact with it as a normal request. Since CONNECT requests aren't supposed to have a normal request or response body this may cause someone to accidently break the request if they weren't paying attention to the CONNECT. E.g. buffering all the data, or responding with HTML.

Responses with a status code of 300+ are allowed to have a body (e.g. for errors), so we need to check the status code when writing.

I noticed that Upgrades only disabled the Stream, not the PipeWriter, so I did something similar there.

Fixes #43697

## Customer Impact

This helps apps avoid accidentally mishandling a CONNECT request.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

New feature area.

issue_context.title: HTTP/2 WebSockets should not allow using the body streams

review_comments: I changed this here and the max value because when Expect fails it's usually because it received a different frame than expected, and the frame length is the least interesting bit of information. I want the checks below for the type and flags to run and then it verifies the length last.
See the discussion at the call site. We're not passing in the value anymore and don't want a low limit by default.

What happens when the endpoint does absolutely nothing for an extended CONNECT request? Just `httpContext => Task.CompletedTask`. Do we just produce an "empty" 200 response? Or a 500? I think it should be a 500 given the request was not successfully handled. Do we log anything about not properly handling an extended CONNECT in this case?

I know that isn't the original issue, but this got me thinking. If we are producing a 200 response this case, I guess this could be addressed in a follow up.

I just tried this. The client gets back a 200, END_STREAM. They might get an additional RST_STREAM frame if the request side of the stream is still open.

I think this is fine. The connection is 'accepted' and immediately closed. Yes the server did this by mistake, but the client isn't left in a bad state.

I chalk this ambiguity up to 200 being a bad choice for an accept status code 😁.
This is something I'd like to revisit based on customer feedback.
